Can You Get Dental Implants After Wearing Dentures for Years?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Many people who have worn dentures for a number of years begin to wonder whether they might still be able to transition to dental implants. Perhaps your dentures have become loose, uncomfortable, or are affecting your confidence when eating or speaking. It is entirely understandable to explore alternatives — and increasingly, long-term denture wearers are asking exactly this question.

Dental implants after years of wearing dentures is a topic that generates a great deal of interest online, partly because the answer is not always straightforward. Several clinical factors need to be assessed before a recommendation can be made, and one of the most significant of these is the health and volume of your jawbone.

This article aims to explain, in plain language, how years of denture wearing can affect your suitability for implants, what the assessment process typically involves, and what options may be available to you. If you are considering this transition, understanding the background will help you have a more informed conversation with your dental team.

Yes, dental implants after years of wearing dentures are often possible, but suitability depends on a clinical assessment. Long-term denture use is associated with jawbone resorption, which may affect implant placement. Where bone loss has occurred, procedures such as bone grafting may be considered. A qualified dental professional can evaluate your individual circumstances.

Why Do People Consider Switching from Dentures to Implants?

Dentures have been a reliable and widely used solution for missing teeth for many decades. However, they do come with limitations that some patients find increasingly difficult to manage over time. Common concerns include:

  • Slipping or movement during eating or speaking, which can cause discomfort or embarrassment
  • Sore spots on the gums caused by friction
  • Difficulty chewing certain foods, particularly harder or chewier items
  • Changes in fit over time as the shape of the jaw changes
  • Impact on confidence, including concerns about the appearance or security of the denture

Dental implants are a different type of tooth replacement. Rather than sitting on top of the gum or relying on adhesive, they are anchored directly into the jawbone, offering a more stable foundation for replacement teeth. For many patients, this increased stability can represent a meaningful improvement in quality of life.

It is important to note that no dental treatment guarantees a specific outcome, and whether implants are suitable for any individual will always depend on a thorough clinical evaluation.

What Happens to the Jawbone When You Wear Dentures?

One of the most important clinical considerations for long-term denture wearers is bone resorption — the gradual loss of jawbone density and volume that occurs when natural tooth roots are no longer present.

Tooth roots play a vital biological role. When you chew and bite, the force is transmitted through the root into the surrounding bone, which stimulates the bone to maintain its density and structure. When a tooth is lost and no root replacement is placed, the bone in that area no longer receives this stimulation and begins to resorb, or shrink, over time.

Conventional dentures sit on the surface of the gum and do not replicate this root stimulation. As a result, the bone beneath the denture continues to resorb throughout the years of denture use. This is one reason why dentures often need periodic relining or replacement — the shape of the jaw gradually changes.

The extent of bone loss varies considerably between individuals and is influenced by factors including the length of time teeth have been missing, overall health, nutrition, and other individual characteristics. This is why a thorough clinical and radiographic assessment is essential before any implant treatment can be planned.

How Bone Loss Affects Implant Suitability

For a dental implant to be placed successfully, there needs to be sufficient bone volume and density at the intended implant site to support and anchor the implant fixture. When long-term bone resorption has reduced the available bone, this can present a clinical challenge.

However, it is important to understand that insufficient bone does not automatically mean implants are impossible. A number of clinical approaches may be considered to address this, including:

Bone Grafting

Bone grafting involves augmenting the existing bone with additional material to create a more suitable foundation for implant placement. The graft material may be sourced from various origins, including synthetic or processed alternatives. After grafting, a period of healing is typically required before implants are placed.

Sinus Lift Procedures

In the upper jaw, bone loss can bring the floor of the sinus cavity very close to the gum line. A sinus lift is a procedure that carefully raises the sinus floor and places bone graft material below it, creating additional bone height for implant placement.

Implant-Supported Overdentures

In some cases, particularly where significant bone loss has occurred, a full set of implants may not be the most appropriate solution. An implant-supported overdenture — sometimes called snap-on dentures — uses a smaller number of implants to anchor and stabilise a denture, rather than replacing it entirely with fixed teeth. This can offer significantly improved stability compared to a conventional denture, even where bone volume is limited.

The most appropriate approach for each patient depends entirely on their individual clinical circumstances, and this can only be determined through proper assessment. You can learn more about the range of dental implant treatments available in London to understand what options may exist.

The Clinical Assessment Process

If you are considering dental implants after long-term denture use, the first step is a comprehensive clinical assessment. This is not simply a brief consultation — it typically involves several components designed to give your dental team a thorough picture of your oral and general health.

Dental and Medical History

Your dental team will want to understand your full dental history, including how long you have been wearing dentures, the reason your natural teeth were lost, and any previous dental treatments. Your general medical history is also highly relevant, as certain health conditions and medications can affect both bone health and the healing process after implant surgery.

Clinical Oral Examination

A thorough examination of your mouth, gums, and remaining teeth (if any) will be carried out. The health of your gum tissue and any signs of gum disease or other oral health conditions will be noted, as these may need to be addressed before implant treatment can begin.

Radiographic Imaging (X-rays and CBCT Scanning)

Conventional dental X-rays provide useful information, but three-dimensional imaging — known as cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scanning — is increasingly used in implant planning. This allows your dental team to assess bone volume, density, and the precise anatomy of your jaw in three dimensions, which is essential for safe and accurate implant planning.

Treatment Planning

Based on all of the above information, your dental team can develop a personalised treatment plan that outlines recommended options, the sequence of any required procedures, expected timescales, and associated costs. This plan should be presented clearly and allow you to ask questions before making any decisions. If you still feel uncertain, seeking a second opinion before dental implants can be a practical next step.

General Health Factors That May Affect Implant Suitability

Bone volume is not the only consideration when assessing suitability for dental implants after years of denture wearing. A number of general health factors are also relevant:

Smoking and tobacco use: Smoking is associated with reduced healing capacity and an increased risk of implant complications. Patients who smoke are not automatically excluded from implant treatment, but the potential impact on outcomes is an important part of the clinical discussion.

Diabetes: Well-managed diabetes is generally not a barrier to implant treatment, but poorly controlled diabetes can impair healing and increase infection risk. Your dental team will want to understand how well your diabetes is managed before proceeding.

Osteoporosis and bone-affecting medications: Some medications used to treat osteoporosis, particularly bisphosphonates, can affect how bone heals following surgical procedures. It is essential to share a full and accurate medication list with your dental team.

Immune system conditions: Certain conditions or medications that affect the immune system may influence healing and should be discussed openly during your assessment.

None of these factors necessarily rules out implant treatment, but they all form part of the full clinical picture that your dental team will need to consider.

What the Transition Process Typically Involves

For those who are deemed suitable for implant treatment following assessment, the process of transitioning from dentures to implants is a journey that typically takes place over several months. The general sequence may include:

  • Initial assessment and treatment planning

as described above

  • Preparatory treatment

addressing any gum disease, infection, or other oral health issues

  • Bone grafting, if required

followed by a healing period, which may last several months

  • Implant placement surgery

a surgical procedure usually carried out under local anaesthetic

  • Osseointegration

the period during which the implant fuses with the surrounding bone, typically several months

  • Placement of the final restoration

the crown, bridge, or fixed arch that sits on top of the implants

Throughout this process, your dental team should keep you informed at each stage, and temporary restorations may be provided so that you are not without teeth during the treatment period.

Oral Health Considerations During and After Treatment

Maintaining good oral health throughout the implant process — and on an ongoing basis afterwards — is an important part of supporting the best possible outcomes. This includes:

  • Thorough daily cleaning around implants using a soft-bristled toothbrush, interdental brushes, and where recommended, floss or water flossers
  • Attending all scheduled review appointments so that your dental team can monitor the health of your implants, gums, and surrounding bone
  • Avoiding smoking where possible, particularly during the healing period
  • Maintaining a balanced diet to support bone health and general healing
  • Wearing any temporary restorations as instructed to avoid placing undue pressure on healing implant sites

Implants, like natural teeth, require consistent care and professional monitoring. They do not decay in the same way as natural teeth, but the gum and bone around them can be affected by a condition called peri-implantitis — a form of inflammation similar to gum disease — if oral hygiene is not maintained.

For those interested in understanding more about long-term care, exploring guidance on implant aftercare and maintenance can be a helpful starting point.

When to Seek a Professional Dental Assessment

If you are a long-term denture wearer and are considering whether implants might be an option for you, there is rarely a need to wait for a specific symptom before seeking a consultation. However, certain experiences may make it particularly timely to arrange an assessment:

  • Your dentures have become noticeably looser or ill-fitting
  • You are experiencing persistent sore spots or discomfort under your dentures
  • You are finding it increasingly difficult to eat a comfortable and varied diet
  • Your dentures are affecting your confidence or quality of life
  • You have noticed changes in your facial appearance, such as a sunken appearance around the mouth, which can be associated with bone resorption

None of these situations represents a dental emergency, but they are all good reasons to seek a professional opinion. A clinical assessment will give you an accurate and personalised picture of where you stand and what options may be appropriate. You can explore dental implant consultations in London to find out what to expect from an initial appointment.

Prevention and Maintaining Oral Health as a Denture Wearer

If you are currently wearing dentures and are not yet ready to consider implants, or if implants are not suitable for your circumstances, there are steps you can take to maintain your oral health and the ongoing fit and comfort of your dentures:

  • Clean your dentures daily using a denture brush and appropriate denture cleaning solution, not regular toothpaste, which can scratch the surface
  • Remove dentures at night to allow your gum tissue to rest
  • Attend regular dental check-ups, even without natural teeth, so that your dentist can monitor your gum health, check for any oral health changes, and assess the fit of your dentures
  • Report any changes in fit promptly, as poorly fitting dentures can cause accelerated bone loss and gum irritation
  • Maintain a healthy and balanced diet to support bone density and general health
  • Stay hydrated, as dry mouth can increase the risk of gum irritation under dentures

Preventative care plays a role in maintaining your oral health regardless of what tooth replacement option you have chosen.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants after years of wearing dentures are often clinically possible, but suitability is always determined on an individual basis through clinical assessment.
  • Long-term denture use is associated with jawbone resorption, which is an important factor in implant planning.
  • Reduced bone volume does not automatically exclude patients from implant treatment; options such as bone grafting may be considered where appropriate.
  • General health factors, including smoking status, diabetes management, and certain medications, are all relevant to implant suitability.
  • The transition from dentures to implants is a multi-stage process that typically takes place over several months.
  • Good oral hygiene and regular dental monitoring are essential for the long-term health of dental implants.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there an age limit for getting dental implants after wearing dentures?

There is no specific upper age limit for dental implants. Suitability is assessed based on overall health, bone quality, and individual clinical factors rather than age alone. Many patients in their 60s, 70s, and beyond have undergone successful implant treatment. Your dental team will carry out a thorough assessment to determine whether implants are appropriate for you, taking into account your full medical and dental history.

How long does the process take from assessment to final teeth?

The timeline varies considerably depending on individual circumstances. Where bone grafting is required, the overall process may take anywhere from 12 to 18 months or more. Without the need for significant preparatory treatment, the timeline may be shorter. Your dental team will provide a personalised estimate as part of your treatment planning, so you have a realistic understanding of what to expect before committing to treatment.

Will I be without teeth at any point during the implant process?

In most cases, your dental team will make arrangements to ensure you have a temporary restoration throughout the treatment process, so you are not left without teeth. The nature of the temporary restoration will depend on your individual treatment plan and the number of implants being placed. This is an important practical point to discuss during your consultation.

Can bone grafting guarantee that implants will be successful?

No dental procedure can guarantee a specific outcome, and bone grafting is no exception. Grafting procedures aim to create a more suitable foundation for implant placement, and many patients proceed successfully to implants following grafting. However, outcomes depend on a wide range of individual factors, including general health, bone healing capacity, and adherence to post-operative care instructions. Your dental team will discuss realistic expectations with you during the planning process.

What is an implant-supported overdenture, and is it different from full implants?

An implant-supported overdenture uses a small number of implants — typically two to four — to anchor and stabilise a denture, rather than replacing each tooth individually with a fixed implant-supported crown or bridge. The overdenture can still be removed for cleaning but is held securely in place during use by attachments that connect to the implants. This option may be particularly relevant where bone volume is limited or where a full fixed implant restoration is not the most suitable approach.

Does it hurt to have dental implants placed?

Implant placement is a surgical procedure, but it is typically carried out under local anaesthetic so you should not feel pain during the procedure itself. Some discomfort, swelling, and bruising in the days following surgery is common and is usually manageable with over-the-counter pain relief as recommended by your dental team. Your team will provide detailed post-operative care instructions and will be available to answer any questions or concerns you have during the recovery period.

Conclusion

For many long-term denture wearers, the question of whether dental implants might be a possibility is a very understandable one. Dentures serve an important function, but they also have limitations that can become more pronounced over time — not least because the bone beneath them continues to change in the absence of tooth roots.

Dental implants after years of wearing dentures are often a realistic clinical option, particularly where a thorough assessment reveals adequate or augmentable bone, good general health, and no unmanaged medical contraindications. Modern implant dentistry, combined with preparatory procedures such as bone grafting where needed, has expanded the range of patients who may benefit from implant-supported restorations.

The most important step for anyone considering this transition is to seek a professional clinical assessment from a suitably qualified and experienced dental team. Only through examination, imaging, and a full review of your health history can an accurate and personalised picture be formed.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

If you have been wearing dentures for a number of years and would like to understand whether implants might be appropriate for you, speaking with a dental professional is a recommended place to begin.
